title: Pressed flower cake decoration
subtitle: using dried pressed flowers to decorate cakes and tarts
excerpt: Edible pressed flowers from a baking supplier, or flowers pressed from your own garden, are layered onto cakes under a thin coat of clear glaze to hold them in place. The look is botanical and delicate, and is particularly suited to naked or semi-naked cakes, cheesecakes, and tarts. The pressing and drying process takes a few days in advance; the decoration itself takes under ten minutes.
sourceNotes: Pressed flower decoration on cakes popularised in British cake decorating from approximately 2015 onward. Edible flower safety guidance from UK Food Standards Agency documentation.

glossaryTerms.definition: Flowers that are safe to consume and that have been pressed flat and dried for decorative use. Common edible varieties include violas, pansies, roses, and chamomile.

content.text: produces a flat, botanical finish that suits rustic, naked, or semi-naked cakes. The flowers must be either purchased from a bakery supplier (already pressed and food-safe) or pressed from known edible varieties grown without pesticides. Never use flowers from a florist, as these are treated with chemicals that are not food-safe.

Only use flowers that are confirmed edible and grown without pesticides. Toxic or chemically treated flowers are the primary risk with this technique. When in doubt, use flowers from a specialist baking supplier rather than picking your own.

Place fresh flowers between two sheets of baking parchment inside a heavy book. Add a few more heavy books on top. Leave for 7 to 10 days in a dry room. The flowers are ready when they are completely flat and papery with no remaining moisture. Violas and pansies are reliable choices; chamomile and cornflowers also press well.
Arrange the pressed flowers on the cake surface (buttercream, fondant, or the top of a tart). Try different placements before committing; moving them once the glaze is applied is much harder.
Once happy with the arrangement, press each flower lightly against the surface with a fingertip so it makes good contact.
Using a clean pastry brush, paint a thin layer of clear piping gel or mirror glaze over each flower to hold it in place and give a slight sheen.
Leave to set for 10 to 15 minutes before moving the cake. The glaze sets firm enough to protect the flowers and keep them in position.

attrs.problem: Flowers lifting or falling off after decoration
attrs.avoid: Avoid a glaze coat that is too thin; a single very light brush may not be enough to hold them.
attrs.fix: Apply a second thin coat of glaze over the flowers once the first has set.

attrs.problem: Flowers losing their colour and turning brown
attrs.avoid: Avoid applying them more than 2 hours before serving; moisture from the cake will eventually discolour them.
attrs.fix: Decorate as close to serving time as practical, particularly for flowers with delicate pigments.
